subtopic_detail: weighing a contested medication association against active suicidal ideation in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17 year old boy who is eight weeks into a course of isotretinoin prescribed by a dermatologist for severe nodulocystic acne that had scarred his cheeks and back.

His mother booked the appointment because he has stopped going to soccer training, spends most of his time in his room and has become monosyllabic at home. Seen alone, he tells you his mood has been flat for about five weeks, that he has stopped enjoying things he used to, and that he sleeps poorly. When you ask directly, he says that in the past fortnight he has sometimes thought that everyone would be better off without him, though he has no plan and has never harmed himself. He had a depressive episode at 15 that responded to psychological therapy alone.

data_table.Examination: Flattened affect with reduced spontaneous speech, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, passive thoughts that others would be better off without him without plan or intent, marked improvement in the acne itself
data_table.Investigations: Liver function within normal limits, fasting lipids within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and review the mood in two weeks time
options.rationale: A dose relationship has not been established for the psychiatric association, so halving the dose has no evidential basis for resolving the problem. It preserves the exposure while delaying definitive action. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the isotretinoin and start an antidepressant at the same visit
options.rationale: Adding a second medication while continuing a drug that requires cessation under its own product information leaves the possible contributor in place and complicates the picture. It also delays the specialist assessment that his suicidal thinking warrants. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the isotretinoin and review him in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: A four week interval is far too long for an adolescent who has expressed thoughts that others would be better off without him. Passive death wishes require assessment within days, not weeks. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Cease the isotretinoin and arrange an urgent mental health assessment
options.rationale: Whatever the strength of the causal evidence at population level, the product information directs cessation if significant mood change or suicidal ideation emerges, and the presence of active passive death wishes in an adolescent with a previous depressive episode makes continuing the drug indefensible. Stopping is reversible and the acne can be reconsidered once he is well. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure that the association is unproven and continue the treatment
options.rationale: It is correct that large cohort studies have not established causation and that severe acne itself carries a substantial risk of depression, so the reasoning behind this option is genuinely sound at population level. That evidence governs whether the drug should be prescribed at all, not what to do for the individual in front of you who has developed suicidal thinking while taking it. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: The relationship between isotretinoin and depression has been debated for three decades and the population level evidence does not establish causation, with large cohort and case crossover studies showing no increase in depression or suicide attributable to the drug, and several suggesting that mood improves as severe acne clears. Severe acne is itself independently associated with depression, social withdrawal and suicidal ideation, which confounds the comparison substantially. Despite this, both Australian product information and prescribing practice require that patients and families be counselled about mood change before starting, that mood be reviewed at each visit, and that the drug be ceased if significant psychiatric symptoms emerge, reflecting the asymmetry between a reversible pause in an elective treatment and the consequences of a missed adolescent depression. The practical skill being tested is holding these two things together: the population evidence determines whether the drug is reasonable to prescribe, while the individual presentation determines what to do next for this patient. Any adolescent expressing thoughts that others would be better off without them requires assessment within days regardless of what medication they are taking.
key_points: Population evidence does not establish a causal link with depression or suicide
Severe acne independently carries a substantial risk of depression, confounding the association
Product information nonetheless directs cessation if significant mood change emerges
Population level evidence governs prescribing, not the response to an individual event
Passive death wishes in an adolescent require assessment within days
explanation.pearls: Counsel about mood and ask about it at every isotretinoin review, and record the conversation, because the obligation to monitor and to cease on significant mood change holds under Australian product information regardless of what the epidemiological evidence shows about causation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: pursuing copper studies when caeruloplasmin sits within the reference range in a young person with psychiatric and movement signs
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23 year old man admitted under your team. Over ten months he has become increasingly irritable and disinhibited, has failed two university semesters after previously doing well, and four months ago was diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis at another hospital.

Risperidone was started at 1 mg daily and within a week he developed marked rigidity and a coarse tremor, which his previous team described as an unusually severe reaction to a low dose. His speech has become slurred over the past two months and his handwriting has shrunk and become untidy. His mother has noticed he drools on his pillow. He drinks alcohol rarely and his urine drug screen is negative. He has one older sister who is well.

data_table.Examination: Dysarthria with hypophonia, coarse proximal tremor of both arms on posture, cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, micrographia, drooling, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin within normal limits, international normalised ratio within normal limits, serum caeruloplasmin 0.21 g/L (0.20 to 0.60), haemoglobin within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the serum caeruloplasmin level in three months and reassess
options.rationale: This treats a result at the very bottom of the reference range as though it excludes the diagnosis, which is the central trap. Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation, oestrogen and pregnancy, and it sits within the reference range in a meaningful minority of affected patients, so a normal value never excludes the condition and repeating it answers nothing. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility sequences
options.rationale: Imaging may show characteristic changes in the basal ganglia and midbrain and is part of the assessment once the diagnosis is being pursued. The appearances are supportive rather than diagnostic and would not distinguish this from other causes of a young onset movement disorder. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Measure the total serum copper concentration on a fasting sample
options.rationale: Total serum copper is misleading because most circulating copper is bound to caeruloplasmin, so the total falls in parallel with the carrier protein and can appear low, normal or high depending on the balance between reduced carrier and increased free copper. It is not used as a diagnostic test. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper content
options.rationale: Hepatic copper quantification remains the reference standard and retains a role when non invasive testing is equivocal, which makes it the strongest competing answer. It is invasive, carries bleeding risk, and is not the appropriate first step when a urine collection and a slit lamp examination will resolve the question in most neurological presentations. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Collect a 24 hour urine sample for quantitative copper excretion
options.rationale: Basal 24 hour urinary copper excretion is the most useful screening test when the diagnosis is suspected in a symptomatic patient and is raised in almost all those with neurological presentations, which is exactly the group this man falls into. Combined with slit lamp examination for corneal rings, which are present in nearly every patient with neurological involvement, it establishes the diagnosis in most cases without invasive testing. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter, causing failure of biliary copper excretion and of copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin, with accumulation in liver, brain, cornea and kidney, and although it is fatal untreated it is treatable, which is why it must be actively excluded in any patient under about 50 presenting with an unexplained movement disorder, unexplained liver disease, or a psychiatric presentation accompanied by either. Psychiatric features are the presenting complaint in around a third and include personality change, disinhibition, mood disturbance and occasionally psychosis, and they characteristically precede the neurological signs. Two findings in this case should redirect the assessment: markedly disproportionate sensitivity to a low dose of a dopamine blocking drug, which reflects pre-existing basal ganglia injury, and mildly deranged transaminases with a normal bilirubin in a young person. The critical diagnostic pitfall is the caeruloplasmin: it is normal in roughly one in ten patients overall and more often in those with active inflammation, so a value within the reference range must never be used to close the question. Basal 24 hour urinary copper excretion above 1.6 micromol per day supports the diagnosis and slit lamp examination for Kayser Fleischer rings is positive in almost all neurological cases.
key_points: Exclude Wilson disease in anyone under 50 with unexplained movement or liver disease
Psychiatric features precede neurological signs in a substantial proportion
Severe extrapyramidal reaction to a low antipsychotic dose is a warning sign
A caeruloplasmin within the reference range does not exclude the diagnosis
Basal 24 hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination establishes most neurological cases
explanation.pearls: Kayser Fleischer rings are present in over 95 per cent of patients with neurological Wilson disease but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone, so a slit lamp examination is close to definitive in exactly the group that reaches a psychiatric or neurology clinic.
